syllabusTopics: Logic and set: statements, logical connectives, truth tables, theorems based on set operations
Real numbers: geometric representation of real numbers, interval, absolute value
Function: domain and range of a function, inverse function, composite function; algebraic (linear, quadratic and cubic) and transcendental (trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic) functions

Curve sketching: odd and even functions, periodicity, symmetry (about origin, X- and Y-axis), monotonicity; graphs of quadratic, cubic and rational functions, trigonometric (asinbx and acosbx), exponential (e^x), logarithmic (lnx)

Matrices and determinants: transpose of a matrix and its properties; minors and cofactors, adjoint, inverse matrix, determinant, properties of determinants (without proof)
Quadratic equation: nature and roots of a quadratic equation, relation between roots and coefficient, formation of a quadratic equation, symmetric roots, one or both roots common
Complex number: imaginary unit, algebra of complex numbers, geometric representation, absolute (modulus) value and conjugate of complex numbers and their properties, square root of a complex number

card.title: Function: domain and range of a function, inverse function

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A **function** assigns exactly one output to each input — the vertical-line test — with a **domain** fixed by the bans: denominator ≠ 0, even-root radicand ≥ 0, log argument > 0, combined by intersection (√(x−2)/(x²−9) lives on [2, 3) ∪ (3, ∞)). The **range** is fastest found by inversion: solve y = f(x) for x and keep feasible y.…

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: x Every function has an inverse. x Only bijective functions have inverses.  ·  x f^-1(x) = 1/f(x). x f^-1 is the inverse function, not reciprocal.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: For f(x) = 1/(x-3) the domain is every real x except 3, and the range is every real y except 0, because 0 is never attained.  ·  x^2 on all of R is not one-to-one and so has no inverse; only the branch x >= 0, or x <= 0, does.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The mirror line*** — swapping x and y in the solved equation reflects the graph across y = x: inputs and outputs trade places.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: x Domain = Range always. x They can be different sets.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Find the domain and the range of a given function, naming the restriction imposed by every radical, denominator and logarithm.  ·  Construct the inverse of a function by writing y = f(x), solving for x in terms of y, then interchanging x and y, and state the domain and range of the inverse.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Domain: list the bans (denominator, radicand, log) and intersect. Inverse: y = f(x), solve, swap. Range via inversion. f o g: inner function first.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Find the inverse of f(x) = (2x + 3)/(x − 1), x ≠ 1, and state the domain of f⁻¹.** — **Construction:** write y = (2x + 3)/(x − 1) and solve for x: y(x − 1) = 2x + 3 ⟹ yx − y = 2x + 3 ⟹ yx − 2x = y + 3 ⟹ x(y − 2) = y + 3 ⟹ **x = (y + 3)/(y − 2)**. Swapping names: **f⁻¹(x) = (x + 3)/(x − 2)**, defined for x ≠ 2.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): If f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x², find (f∘g)(x) and (g∘f)(x) and deduce that composition is not commutative.** — **(f∘g)(x) = f(g(x))** — apply g first: f(x²) = 2x² + 1. **(g∘f)(x) = g(f(x))** — apply f first: g(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)² = 4x² + 4x + 1.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: For inverse questions, verify by composing: f(f^-1(x)) = x - one line, full marks for confirmation.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Inverses need uniqueness backwards: one-to-one is the exact condition that lets every output be traced back to a single input.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Function: exactly one output per input (vertical-line test). Domain rules: polynomials all R; rational denominator != 0; even roots radicand >= 0; log argument > 0; combinations intersect the conditions. Range = set of outputs; fastest route: solve y = f(x) for x and keep feasible y.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Encryption is a function with a public forward direction and a secret inverse: one-to-one is what makes decryption unambiguous.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Find the domain of f(x) = √(x − 2)/(x² − 9).** — **Condition 1 (even root):** x − 2 ≥ 0 ⟹ x ≥ 2. **Condition 2 (denominator):** x² − 9 ≠ 0 ⟹ x ≠ 3 and x ≠ −3.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Machines With Rules A **function** is a machine assigning exactly one output to each input. The theorems: **domain conventions** (denominators, even roots, logarithms), **composition** f∘g, and the **inverse theorem** — f⁻¹ exists exactly when f is one-to-one, and y = f(x) ⟺ x = f⁻¹(y).  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 Definition and testing - **Function f: A → B:** every a ∈ A has **exactly one** image f(a) ∈ B. Vertical-line test: any vertical line cuts the graph at most once. - **Domain** = allowed inputs; **range** = actual outputs {f(x) : x ∈ D}. ### 2.2 Domain theorems - **Polynomials:** all of ℝ. **Rational:** denominator ≠ 0.…  ·  ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Function** | Exactly one output per input | f(x) = x² | | **Composite** | f(g(x)) — chain of machines | √(1 − x²) | | **One-to-one** | Distinct inputs, distinct outputs | eˣ, ln x | | **Inverse** | Undoing machine: f⁻¹(f(x)) = x | f⁻¹ of eˣ is ln x |

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: For f(x) = (x+1)/(x-1) one finds f(f(x)) = x, so the function is its own inverse and f^-1 = f.  ·  A constant function on a set with more than one element is onto its image but not one-to-one, so it has no inverse.  ·  Restricting the domain of f shrinks its range, and that is exactly what can turn it into the whole codomain and create an inverse.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: No verified PYQ on this row exists in the bank; all items here are NEB-style practice.  ·  "f has an inverse iff f is one-to-one; (f o g)(x) = f(g(x)); the graph of f^-1 is f's graph reflected in y = x."  ·  Find the inverse of f(x) = (2x + 3)/(x − 1) and its domain.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Compute f∘g and g∘f for f(x) = 2x + 1, g(x) = x².  ·  Find the domain of √(x − 2)/(x² − 9).  ·  Use the horizontal line test to decide whether a function is one-to-one, and hence whether an inverse can exist on the given domain.

rows.text: Evaluate composite functions such as f o g and f o f, and test which of the two compositions returns the identity function.  ·  Sketch a function and its inverse on the same axes, drawing the line y = x as the mirror line and labelling matched points.  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why inverses need one-to-one - An inverse must send each output back to a **unique** input. If f(a) = f(b) with a ≠ b, the inverse cannot decide where to send the common value — ambiguity kills invertibility.…

rows.text: ## 5. Comparison Tables **Function vs relation** | Basis | Function | General relation | |---|---|---| | outputs per input | exactly one | any number | | vertical-line test | passes | may fail | | inverse | needs one-to-one | always a relation |  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **f⁻¹ means inverse, not reciprocal:** 1/f is a new function; f⁻¹ undoes f — different objects entirely.  ·  **Composition order:** (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)) — g acts **first**; reading left-to-right as "f then g" is the classic error.
